---
title: "P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget"
---

## The question

A well-lit leaf exports sugar while a root consumes it. What connects the two,
and why can the same leaf release CO2 in darkness? Explain energy capture,
carbon fixation, transport, respiration and nutrient assimilation. Interpret a
response without assuming that light is its only limitation.

## Capturing energy differs from fixing carbon

Pigments in chloroplast thylakoids absorb light. Excitation reaches reaction
centres, and electron transfer supports a proton electrochemical gradient.
ATP synthase uses that gradient to form ATP. Water supplies electrons to
photosystem II and oxygen is released; photosynthetic oxygen does not come
directly from splitting CO2.

Linear electron flow supports ATP and NADPH formation. Cyclic flow can
contribute additional ATP without equivalent net NADPH or oxygen production.
ATP and reducing power are intermediate resources, not the final carbohydrate
supply for the entire plant. Their production must be coordinated with use.

The Calvin–Benson cycle operates in the stroma. Rubisco adds CO2 to ribulose
bisphosphate. Subsequent reactions use ATP and NADPH to reduce the products;
some carbon becomes available for synthesis and export while the rest
regenerates the acceptor. In standard cycle accounting, three fixed CO2 and
nine ATP plus six NADPH support one net triose-phosphate equivalent. This
does not represent every energetic cost of building a plant.

“Dark reactions” is a misleading name. These reactions do not consume photons
directly, but light-dependent resources and regulation support them. Ordinary
carbon fixation cannot continue indefinitely in darkness just because the
cycle is described as light-independent.

## Oxygenation imposes additional costs

Rubisco can react with oxygen instead of CO2. The resulting photorespiratory
pathway recovers carbon while releasing some CO2 and consuming energy. It
involves chloroplasts, peroxisomes and mitochondria. Photorespiration is distinct
from mitochondrial respiration, even though both can contribute CO2 release.
Under relevant conditions, warming and reduced internal CO2 favour a greater
relative oxygenation rate.

Water stress can close stomata and reduce CO2 supply. Net uptake may decline
despite bright light. Later limitations may involve metabolism or tissue
damage. A lower measured rate alone cannot identify stomatal, photochemical
or biochemical limitation. It is an integrated outcome requiring more evidence.

## C3, C4 and CAM change carbon delivery

In C3 plants, initial Rubisco products are three-carbon compounds. C4 plants
first capture inorganic carbon through PEP carboxylase into four-carbon
compounds. In the common two-cell arrangement, these compounds release CO2
near Rubisco in bundle-sheath cells. Concentrating CO2 can suppress
photorespiration but costs additional energy. Warm, bright conditions often
favour this strategy; it is not universally superior.

CAM plants commonly take up CO2 at night and store carbon in organic acids,
then release it for fixation during the day. Separating these steps in time
can reduce water loss. Storage and rate constraints remain. C4 and CAM deliver
concentrated CO2 to the Calvin–Benson cycle rather than replacing it.

Predict different evidence for each hypothesis. A nocturnal rise in acid
content informs a CAM hypothesis; anatomy and gas-exchange responses inform
a C4 hypothesis. A single observation may not establish the entire pathway.
Some species show intermediate or flexible behaviour.

## A response curve describes a balance

Net CO2 exchange balances uptake and release under the measurement conditions.
At low light, increased irradiance can increase net uptake. The light
compensation point is the condition at which uptake and release balance.
At greater light, CO2 supply, biochemical capacity or another process can
become limiting. Excess excitation can be dissipated protectively; damage
exceeding repair can cause photoinhibition.

Imagine invented net rates of −2, 0, 6 and 9 µmol CO2 m⁻² s⁻¹ at 0, 50,
200 and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Compensation is near the second observation.
The smaller response per additional photon at high light does not prove which
process limits it. Record temperature, CO2, humidity, leaf age and measurement
order. Repeated conditions on one leaf are not separate independent plants.

Pigment concentration, chlorophyll fluorescence and CO2 exchange measure
different properties. Fluorescence informs photochemical behaviour, whereas
net gas exchange includes additional processes. A greener leaf need not have
proportionally greater carbon uptake.

## Sources and sinks change with development

A **source** exports assimilate; a **sink** imports it for use or storage.
A mature illuminated leaf is commonly a source and a root or developing fruit
a sink. A storage organ can become a source during regrowth. These are current
carbon roles rather than immutable organ identities.

Phloem loading raises solute content near a source, favouring water entry and
pressure development. Unloading and carbon use at sinks help maintain a
pressure difference driving bulk flow. Species differ in loading routes.
Different tubes can carry assimilate in different directions, so phloem is
not simply an exclusively downward counterpart to xylem.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  light[Illuminated mature leaf] --> suc[Sucrose loading]
  suc --> pressure[Water entry and source pressure]
  pressure --> flow[Phloem bulk flow]
  flow --> young[Growing organs]
  flow --> store[Storage organs]
  store -->|During remobilisation| export[New source supplying growth]
```

This original schematic separates carbon roles from organ location. It omits
many transport steps and does not imply that every species loads identically.

Starch can bridge day and night. Storage, export and growth demand are
regulated together; reduced sink demand can change source activity. Transport
is not independent of flowering, seed filling or senescence.

## Respiration supplies more than CO2

Glycolysis, the tricarboxylic-acid cycle and mitochondrial electron transport
connect carbohydrate breakdown to ATP and metabolic intermediates. Plants
respire in light and darkness. Roots use carbon for uptake, maintenance and
growth; leaves also require mitochondrial function. Respiration is not merely
wasteful reversal of photosynthesis.

When oxygen is restricted, oxidative ATP generation is limited. Fermentation
can regenerate NAD+ and permit continued glycolysis, with much lower ATP yield
than complete aerobic oxidation. Waterlogged roots can therefore develop
energy and transport limitations despite well-lit leaves. Many seeds also use
lipid reserves during establishment, connecting reserve mobilisation and
organelle metabolism to developmental stage.

Nitrate must be reduced before incorporation into organic nitrogen. Ammonium
assimilation requires carbon skeletons and energy. Nutrient supply can alter
photosynthetic capacity, while carbon supply can limit nutrient assimilation.
Whole-plant budgets require both sides. More nitrogen cannot necessarily
compensate for inadequate light or lack of oxygen at roots.
